title: Power from the Sun
summary: How solar panels turn sunlight into electricity, why sunny countries like Saudi Arabia are building solar farms, and the challenges of dust, heat, and darkness.
poll: Sunny countries should get most of their electricity from the sun.

versions.title: Power from the Sun
versions.text:
The sun is hot. It is bright. It gives us light. It can give us power, too!

Have you seen a solar panel? Look on a roof. It is flat. It is dark. It sits in the sun all day. It makes electricity from the sun's light. That runs lights and fans.

Saudi Arabia gets lots of sun. So do the lands near it. Now big solar farms sit in the sand. They have rows and rows of them. Some homes have panels on top, too.

Solar power is clean. It makes no smoke. And the sun will not run out. It will shine for a long, long time. We can use it each day.

But there are problems. Wind blows dust. It gets on all things. The dust lands on the panels. Then they make less power. So they must be cleaned. Men do this job. Robots do it, too.

At night, there is no sun. They stop. So we save some from the day. We keep it in big batteries. Then we use it at night. The lights stay on!

The sun is a huge ball of hot gas. Each day, it sends us light and heat. Now we can turn that light into power.

A solar panel is a flat, dark board. It has lots of small parts called cells. The sun shines on the cells. Then they make electricity. It can run lights and fans. It can even run air conditioners.

Some lands get much more sun than the rest. Saudi Arabia gets strong sun most of the year. So do the lands next to it. That is why huge solar farms are being built in the desert. Each one has rows and rows of panels. There are thousands! Some homes and schools have panels on top, too.

Solar power is clean. It makes no smoke. And the sun will not run out.

Still, solar power has problems. Strong winds blow dust. The dust lands on the panels. Then the panels make less power. So they must be cleaned. Some are cleaned by robots.

At night, the panels make none at all. So we save some from the day. We keep it in big batteries. Then we can use it when it is dark.

versions.title: Power from the Sun
versions.text:
The sun is a giant ball of hot gas. It glows. Each day, it sends lots of light and heat to Earth. Today, people are learning to turn that light into electricity.

A solar panel is a flat, dark board. It is made of many small solar cells. Most of these cells are made from sand. The sand has been changed in a special way. Sunlight hits the cells. Then they make power. This power can run lights and computers. It can run air conditioners, too.

Some places get much more sun than others. Saudi Arabia and its neighbors have strong sun on most days of the year. That is why huge solar farms are now being built in the desert there. Each farm has thousands of panels. They are lined up in long rows. Some homes and schools have panels on their roofs as well.

Solar power has lots of good points. Solar power is clean. It makes no smoke. The sun will keep shining for billions of years. So it will not run out.

But solar power also has problems. Strong winds blow dust onto the panels. Dusty panels make less power. So workers and robots must clean them often.

Night is a problem, too. When the sun goes down, the panels stop working. To solve this, we can save extra power from the day. It goes in large batteries. Then it can be used after dark.

versions.title: Power from the Sun

The sun is a giant ball of glowing gas. Each day, it sends huge amounts of light and heat to Earth. Scientists and engineers have found a way to catch some of that light. They turn it into electricity.

A solar panel is a flat, dark board. It is covered with many small solar cells. Most cells are made of silicon. Silicon comes from sand. Sunlight strikes the cells. Then they make power. This power can run lights and computers. It also runs the air conditioners that keep homes cool in summer.

Some places get much more sunshine than others. Saudi Arabia and its neighbors have strong sun on almost every day of the year. So the region is a great place for solar power. Very large solar farms are now being built in the desert. Each one has thousands of panels. They are lined up in rows. Panels are also showing up on the roofs of homes and schools.

Solar power has some big advantages. Solar power is clean. It makes no smoke when it makes power. And the sun will keep shining for billions of years. So this energy will not run out.

Solar power also has some problems. Strong winds blow dust onto the panels. A dusty panel makes less power. So workers and cleaning robots must wipe the panels often.

Night brings another problem. Panels can't work without sunlight. One answer is to store extra power from the day in large batteries. That way, people can use it after dark.

versions.title: Power from the Sun
versions.text:
The sun is a giant ball of glowing gas. Each day it sends a huge amount of energy to Earth. The energy comes as light and heat. For a long time, most of the world's power came from burning oil, gas, and coal. Now more and more countries are learning to convert sunlight straight into electricity.

A solar panel is a flat, dark board. It is covered with rows of small solar cells. Most cells are made of silicon, which comes from sand. When sunlight strikes a cell, it makes a small electric current. Many cells working together make enough power to run lights, computers, and air conditioners.

Some places get far more sun than others. Saudi Arabia and its neighbors have strong sun almost every day of the year. They also have wide, open deserts with plenty of space. As a result, huge solar farms are being built across the region. Each has thousands of panels. Saudi Arabia has set a goal for the year 2030. It wants to make about half of its power from renewable sources, such as sunlight and wind.

Solar power has clear benefits. It is renewable, which means it will not run out. The sun will shine for billions of years. Solar power also makes no smoke or air pollution while it makes power.

Yet solar power faces some challenges. Desert winds blow dust onto the panels. Dusty panels make less power. So engineers have built cleaning robots with soft brushes. These robots sweep the panels without using precious water.

Night is another challenge. Panels make nothing in the dark. Large batteries can provide storage for extra energy made during the day. Then it can be used after sunset.

A solar panel is a flat, dark board. It is covered with rows of small solar cells. Most of these cells are made of silicon, a material produced from sand. When sunlight strikes a cell, it creates a small electric current. When many cells work together, they make enough power to run lights and computers. Darkness is another challenge, since panels make nothing at night. Large batteries can provide storage for extra energy collected during the day. Then it can be used after sunset. As storage gets better, sunshine may power more and more of our lives.

versions.title: Power from the Sun
versions.text:
The sun is an immense ball of glowing gas. Each day, it sends a tremendous amount of energy to Earth in the form of light and heat. For generations, most of the world's electricity was produced by burning fossil fuels such as oil, natural gas, and coal. Today, however, a growing number of nations are learning to convert sunlight directly into electricity. The change is happening faster than many experts once thought it would.

A solar panel is a flat, dark board covered with rows of small solar cells. Most of these cells are made of silicon, a material that is produced from sand. When sunlight strikes a cell, it generates a small electric current. When many cells work together, they produce enough power to run lights, computers, and the air conditioners that people rely on during the long and scorching summers.

Certain regions receive much more sunshine than others. Saudi Arabia and its neighbors have intense sunlight on nearly every day of the year, and they also have vast, open deserts with plenty of space for large projects. As a result, enormous solar farms holding thousands of panels are being built throughout the region. Saudi Arabia has set an ambitious goal of producing about half of its power from renewable sources, such as sunlight and wind, by 2030.

Solar power offers significant benefits. It is renewable, which means it will not run out, because the sun will keep on shining for billions of years. It also produces no smoke or air pollution while it makes power, and the price of solar panels has dropped sharply over the past few decades, which has made them far more affordable.

Nevertheless, solar power faces serious challenges. Desert winds leave layers of dust on the panels. Dusty panels produce much less power. To address this problem, engineers have designed cleaning robots with soft brushes that sweep the panels without wasting any of the desert's precious water.

Darkness presents another challenge, since panels produce nothing at night. Large batteries can provide storage for surplus energy collected during daylight hours, so that people can use it after sunset. As storage technology continues to improve, sunshine may one day power a growing share of our daily lives.

versions.title: Power from the Sun
versions.text:
The sun is an immense sphere of glowing gas. Every day, it delivers a tremendous quantity of energy to Earth as light and heat. For generations, most of the world's electricity was produced by burning fossil fuels such as oil, natural gas, and coal. Today, however, a growing number of nations are learning to convert sunlight directly into electricity. Few places are better suited to this technology than the Arabian Peninsula.

Most solar panels rely on photovoltaic cells, a name that combines a word meaning "light" with the volt, a unit of electricity. These cells are usually made of silicon, a material refined from sand. When sunlight strikes a cell, its energy loosens tiny particles called electrons. Their movement creates an electric current. Connecting many cells together produces enough power for lights, computers, and the air conditioners that are essential during scorching summers.

Saudi Arabia and its neighbors receive abundant sunshine on nearly every day of the year. They also possess vast deserts with ample room for equipment. Consequently, enormous solar farms containing thousands of panels are being constructed throughout the region. Saudi Arabia has announced a goal of generating approximately half of its electricity from renewable sources, such as sunlight and wind, by 2030.

Solar energy offers significant benefits. It is renewable, since the sun will continue shining for billions of years. It also produces no smoke or air pollution while generating electricity. The cost of panels has also fallen dramatically in recent decades.

Nevertheless, solar power confronts serious challenges. Dust tends to accumulate on panels, blocking sunlight and reducing their output. Because water is scarce in the desert, engineers have designed robots with soft brushes that clean panels without it. Extreme heat creates another difficulty, since panels actually lose some efficiency as they become very hot.

The greatest challenge is that solar power is intermittent: panels produce nothing at night and less on cloudy days. Large batteries can store surplus energy collected during daylight hours for use after sunset. As storage technology improves, sunshine may supply a growing share of the region's power.

versions.title: Power from the Sun
versions.text:
The sun is an immense sphere of incandescent gas. Every day, it delivers a tremendous quantity of energy to Earth in the form of light and heat. For generations, the majority of the world's electricity was produced by combusting fossil fuels such as petroleum, natural gas, and coal. Today, however, an increasing number of nations are learning to convert sunlight directly into electricity. Few locations are better suited to this technology than the Arabian Peninsula.

Most solar panels rely on photovoltaic cells, a designation that combines a Greek word meaning "light" with the volt, a unit of electrical measurement. These cells are typically manufactured from silicon, a material refined from sand. When sunlight strikes a cell, its energy dislodges microscopic particles called electrons. Their movement produces an electric current. Connecting numerous cells together generates sufficient power for illumination, computers, and the air conditioners that are indispensable during scorching summers.

Saudi Arabia and its neighbors receive abundant sunshine on nearly every day of the year. They also possess extensive deserts with ample room for equipment. Consequently, enormous solar installations containing thousands of panels are being constructed throughout the region. Saudi Arabia has announced an ambitious objective of generating approximately half of its electricity from renewable sources, including sunlight and wind, by 2030.

Solar energy offers significant advantages. It is renewable, since the sun will continue radiating energy for billions of years. It also generates no smoke or atmospheric pollution while producing electricity. The cost of photovoltaic panels has also declined dramatically in recent decades, making the technology increasingly affordable for governments, businesses, and individual households.

Nevertheless, solar power confronts considerable challenges. Dust tends to accumulate on panels, obstructing sunlight and substantially diminishing their output. Because water is scarce in desert environments, engineers have developed robotic cleaners with soft brushes that maintain panels without it. Extreme heat introduces an additional complication, since panels actually sacrifice some efficiency as their temperature rises.

The most fundamental challenge is that solar power is intermittent: panels produce nothing at night and less on cloudy days. Large batteries can preserve surplus energy accumulated during daylight hours for consumption after sunset. As storage technology continues to advance, sunshine may supply an expanding proportion of the region's electricity.

versions.title: Power from the Sun
versions.text:
The sun is an immense sphere of incandescent gas that delivers a tremendous quantity of energy to Earth every day in the form of electromagnetic radiation, primarily light and heat. For generations, the overwhelming majority of the world's electricity was produced by combusting fossil fuels such as petroleum, natural gas, and coal. Today, however, an increasing number of nations are learning to convert sunlight directly into electricity. Few locations are more ideally suited to this technology than the Arabian Peninsula.

Most solar panels rely on photovoltaic cells, a designation that combines a Greek word meaning "light" with the volt, a unit of electrical measurement. These cells are typically manufactured from silicon, a semiconducting material refined from sand. When sunlight strikes a cell, its energy dislodges microscopic particles called electrons. Their organized movement produces an electric current. Interconnecting numerous cells generates sufficient power for illumination, computers, and the air conditioning systems that are indispensable during scorching summers.

Saudi Arabia and its neighbors receive abundant sunshine on nearly every day of the year. They also possess extensive deserts with ample territory for equipment. Consequently, enormous solar installations containing thousands of panels are being constructed throughout the region. Saudi Arabia has announced an ambitious objective of generating approximately half of its electricity from renewable sources, including sunlight and wind, by 2030.

Solar energy offers substantial advantages. It is renewable, since the sun will continue radiating energy for billions of years, and it generates no smoke or atmospheric pollution while producing electricity. The cost of photovoltaic panels has also declined dramatically during recent decades, rendering the technology increasingly affordable for governments, businesses, and individual households.

Nevertheless, solar power confronts considerable obstacles. Dust tends to accumulate on panels, obstructing sunlight and substantially diminishing their output. Because water is exceptionally scarce in desert environments, engineers have developed robotic cleaners with soft brushes that maintain panels without consuming it. Extreme heat introduces an additional complication, since photovoltaic panels paradoxically sacrifice some efficiency as their operating temperature rises.

The most fundamental limitation is that solar power is intermittent: panels produce nothing at night and less on cloudy days. Large-scale battery systems can preserve surplus energy accumulated during daylight hours for consumption after sunset. As storage technology continues to advance, sunshine may supply an expanding proportion of the region's electricity.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?

How people use sunlight to make power, and the problems they face
Why the sun is hot and bright
How robots are made in factories
questions.why: The article explains how solar panels turn sunlight into power, where they are built, their good points, and problems like dust and night.

wrong.A: The article is about making power from sunlight, not about building cool houses.
wrong.C: The sun being hot is only a starting point, not the main idea.
wrong.D: Robots are mentioned only as panel cleaners.

questions.stem: What does a solar panel do?

It keeps a house cool by blocking the sun.
It stores water for the desert.
It makes the sun shine brighter.

wrong.B: Panels make power; the article does not say they are used for shade.
wrong.D: Nothing on Earth can make the sun brighter.

The panel makes more power.
The panel makes less power.
The panel works only at night.

wrong.B: Dust blocks sunlight, so power goes down, not up.
wrong.D: Panels do not work at night at all.
